column4: The source-section root ح س ب (accounting) meets its turning-away scene here: the account has drawn near while people are heedlessly turning away (مُّعْرِضُونَ).
A Lord's sign comes to them (تأتيهم), yet they turn away from it; this joins the image's arriving report to the refusal that follows.
Truth came to them and was denied, then the reports they mocked will come to them (جاءهم ... يأتيهم); rejection does not prevent the later arrival.
The source-section root ء ت ي is used for the Hour coming suddenly while its people are unaware (تَأْتِيهِمُ السَّاعَةُ بَغْتَةً), pairing two arrivals as the commentary does.
The source-section root و ل ي names turning toward or away; Pharaoh is told that the one who lies and turns away (كَذَّبَ وَتَوَلَّىٰ) faces punishment.
The one reminded of the Lord's signs then turns away (أَعْرَضَ عَنْهَا) and meets retribution, making the image's refusal and punishment explicit.
The source-section act of turning away appears here as أعرضوا: if people turn away, the Prophet is not their guardian and has only to convey, matching 88:21-23's reminder and limit.
After disbelief, their return is to God, who will inform them of their deeds (إِلَيْنَا مَرْجِعُهُمْ فَنُنَبِّئُهُم); the verse directly joins return to account.
The next ayah completes that sequence with brief enjoyment followed by being driven to severe punishment; its contribution is the fate after the return-and-report in 31:23.
The source-section root ء و ب is used here: The source-section's secondary sense of awāb as a willing return to God is made an explicit choice: whoever wills may take a return to his Lord (مَآبًا).
The source-section root ء و ب gives the return-word ma'ab; here it names the destination for transgressors (مَآبًا), beside 78:39's chosen way to the Lord.
The return becomes an invitation to a willing soul: “Return to your Lord” (ارْجِعِي إِلَىٰ رَبِّكِ), pleased and pleasing, matching the section's voluntary branch of return.
The source's return to a settled destination is stated as “to your Lord is the return” (إِلَىٰ رَبِّكَ الرُّجْعَىٰ), countering any idea that turning away changes where one ends.
The section's claim that the return destination is fixed is repeated in “to Us is the final destination” (إِلَيْنَا الْمَصِيرُ).
A lesser punishment comes before the greater one “so that they might return” (لَعَلَّهُمْ يَرْجِعُونَ); it supplies the interval in which turning back is still possible.
The source-section root ء ت ي is used here: The Hour is coming and each soul will be recompensed for what it strives for; this joins arrival to the accounting that follows 88:25.
After declaring that each person bears their own burden, the verse says “to your Lord is your return” and He will inform you of your disagreements; return and account are adjacent.
On the day people are returned to God, He will tell them what they did (يَوْمَ يُرْجَعُونَ إِلَيْهِ فَيُنَبِّئُهُم); this directly parallels return followed by reckoning.
The warning says people will be returned to God and each soul paid for what it earned (تُرْجَعُونَ فِيهِ إِلَى اللَّهِ); no one can turn away from that accounting.
Even after disbelief, “to Him is your return” and He will inform you of your deeds (إِلَيْهِ مَرْجِعُكُمْ); the verse preserves the order of return then account.
After people are rescued at sea and then transgress, their return is to God, who informs them of their deeds; escape from danger does not alter the destination.
Even in the painful case of parents urging their child to associate others with God, the return is to God, who will report the deeds; human ties do not change the final return.
Turning away from God's reminder (أَعْرَضَ عَن ذِكْرِي) is followed by a constricted life, a specific consequence for the image's act of turning away.

The source-section root و ل ي is used here: The Prophet is told to turn from the one who turns away from the reminder and wants only worldly life (تَوَلَّىٰ عَن ذِكْرِنَا); the preposition and sense match the section's dictionary note.

The source-section root و ل ي is used here: The wretched person is defined as one who denied and turned away (كَذَّبَ وَتَوَلَّىٰ), then is kept from the Fire's opposite; this closely matches the image's paired refusal and consequence.
The source-section root و ل ي is used here: The Fire calls the one who turned his back and turned away (أَدْبَرَ وَتَوَلَّىٰ); the doubled retreat gives a vivid counterpart to the inescapable return.
People are commanded to turn back to their Lord before punishment comes (أَنِيبُوا إِلَىٰ رَبِّكُمْ); this gives the voluntary return its urgent, still-open moment.
Every person labors toward the Lord and will meet Him (فَمُلَاقِيهِ); whatever their present direction, the meeting cannot be avoided.
The next verses begin the outcome of that meeting with a person given the record in the right hand; this row contributes the favorable recipient in the accounting scene.
The source-section root ح س ب appears in this person's easy reckoning (حِسَابًا يَسِيرًا), a direct counterpart to the account laid upon God in 88:26.
After that reckoning, the person returns to their family joyful (يَنقَلِبُ إِلَىٰ أَهْلِهِ مَسْرُورًا), joining return with the glad state of 88:9.
The contrasting recipient is given the record behind his back (وَرَاءَ ظَهْرِهِ), making bodily reversal part of the unfavorable accounting scene.
The person given the record behind his back calls for destruction; this is the next consequence after the unfavorable account begun in 84:10.
The sequence ends with entry into the Blaze, completing the punished return that contrasts with 84:9's joyful return.

The source-section root ء و ب is used here: Paradise is brought near for every “returning, guarding” person (أَوَّابٍ حَفِيظٍ); awāb is the very source-section form for one who repeatedly returns to God.
The source-section root ء و ب is used here: David is praised as “one who often returns” (أَوَّابٌ); this gives a Qur'anic example of the source's voluntary awāb sense.
The source-section root ء و ب is used here: Solomon too is called “one who often returns” (أَوَّابٌ), extending the source's positive return-word to another servant of God.
This neighboring call identifies the addressee as the reassured soul (النَّفْسُ الْمُطْمَئِنَّةُ), explaining why 89:28's return is welcomed.
After the return in 89:28, the soul is told to enter among God's servants (فَادْخُلِي فِي عِبَادِي); this completes the destination's welcome.
The next command is to enter God's Garden (وَادْخُلِي جَنَّتِي), completing the willing return's destination.
When a surah is revealed, some look at one another and then turn away (انصَرَفُوا); revelation arrives, but its hearers withdraw.
The people had the Lord's signs recited to them, yet turned back on their heels (تُنكَصُونَ); this gives a bodily reversal in response to reminder.
The next ayah describes their arrogant, nighttime talk; it supplies the posture accompanying the turning back in 23:66.
The verse condemns the person reminded of the Lord's signs who turns away from them (أَعْرَضَ عَنْهَا), echoing reminder followed by refusal.
The source-section root و ل ي is used here: Whoever turns away from the Messenger is outside the Prophet's guardianship; the verse shares 88:21-22's limit on the messenger's role.
Some turn back after guidance has become clear (ارْتَدُّوا عَلَىٰ أَدْبَارِهِمْ); this is a reversal from guidance rather than the final return to God.
The source-section root و ل ي is used here: The deaf cannot hear the call when they turn their backs and depart (تَوَلَّوْا مُدْبِرِينَ), a concrete refusal of a message.

The source-section root و ل ي is used here: The Prophet “turned away” (تَوَلَّىٰ) from a seeker; unlike 88:23's disbelieving refusal, this different stance shows that the verb itself names turning away, while context determines its moral force.
The blind man had come to the Prophet (جَاءَهُ الْأَعْمَىٰ); his arrival completes 80:1's striking scene of someone coming as another turns away.
The source-section root و ج ه is defined through the place one faces; wherever you turn, there is the Face of God (فَأَيْنَمَا تُوَلُّوا فَثَمَّ وَجْهُ اللَّهِ).
The source-section root و ج ه is explicit in “for each is a direction toward which it turns” (وِجْهَةٌ هُوَ مُوَلِّيهَا); the verse then directs people toward good deeds.
The source-section root و ج ه appears as Abraham directs his face toward the Creator (وَجَّهْتُ وَجْهِيَ), making bodily orientation an explicit turning toward God.
The source-section root و ج ه appears in the command to set one's face toward the upright religion (فَأَقِمْ وَجْهَكَ), a chosen religious orientation.
The source-section root و ج ه appears in the command to set the face toward the upright religion (فَأَقِمْ وَجْهَكَ), developing orientation as a deliberate direction of life.

The source-section root و ج ه appears in the command to set the face toward the upright religion before a day from God arrives that cannot be averted; chosen orientation stands against an unavoidable day.
The source-section root و ج ه appears as the Prophet turns his face toward the Sacred Mosque (فَوَلِّ وَجْهَكَ), a concrete qibla scene for the face-as-direction gloss.
The source-section root و ج ه is used here: The qibla instruction continues: wherever the Prophet goes out, he must turn his face toward the Sacred Mosque; this repeats the direction in 2:144.

The source-section root و ج ه is used here: The same direction is required wherever the believers come from, so that people have no argument against them; it completes the qibla scene with its boundary.
The source-section root و ج ه is used here: The one who submits his face to God (أَسْلَمَ وَجْهَهُ لِلَّهِ) supplies the positive pole to turning away: orientation can embody submission.

The source-section root و ج ه is used here: The best way is described as submitting one's face to God (أَسْلَمَ وَجْهَهُ لِلَّهِ) and following Abraham, again making face-direction a chosen allegiance.
The source-section root و ج ه is used here: The person worshipping on an edge turns on his face when tested (انقَلَبَ عَلَىٰ وَجْهِهِ); the reversal ends in loss of both this life and the next.
The source-section root و ج ه appears in a boundary: righteousness is not simply turning faces east or west (تُوَلُّوا وُجُوهَكُمْ), so outward direction alone is not the measure.
The source-section root و ج ه is used here: The Day's faces are radiant (وُجُوهٌ يَوْمَئِذٍ نَّاضِرَةٌ), a parallel to the contrasting faces and outcomes surrounding 88:2.
Those faces look toward their Lord (إِلَىٰ رَبِّهَا نَاظِرَةٌ); this gives the radiant face in 75:22 a directed, hopeful orientation.
The source-section root و ج ه is used here: The other faces are gloomy (وُجُوهٌ يَوْمَئِذٍ بَاسِرَةٌ), a direct contrary face-state to the radiant group and to 88:8-9.
The gloomy faces expect a backbreaking calamity; this next ayah completes the unfavorable face-state introduced in 75:24.
The source-section root و ج ه is used here: The other surah's final scene begins with faces bright and shining (وُجُوهٌ يَوْمَئِذٍ مُّسْفِرَةٌ), paralleling the two face-groups of al-Ghashiya.
Those bright faces are laughing and joyful (ضَاحِكَةٌ مُّسْتَبْشِرَةٌ); this gives the favorable face in 80:38 its response.
The source-section root و ج ه is used here: The contrasting faces are covered in dust (وُجُوهٌ يَوْمَئِذٍ عَلَيْهَا غَبَرَةٌ), a grim counterpart to the bright faces and to 88:2's humbled faces.
Darkness overwhelms the dusty faces (تَرْهَقُهَا قَتَرَةٌ), completing the visual contrast begun in 80:40.
The final ayah identifies this latter group as disbelieving, wicked people; it completes the face-scene's link between outward state and rejection.
The source-section root ء ت ي is used when the Hour comes upon people only suddenly (تَأْتِيكُمُ السَّاعَةُ إِلَّا بَغْتَةً), echoing the image's unexpected arrival.
When the Hour comes suddenly, the deniers regret their neglect; this gives the sudden arrival in 12:107 its concrete consequence.
The source-section root ء ت ي appears in the warning that the Hour may come suddenly while people are unaware, another direct arrival formulation.
The source-section root ء ت ي appears in the question whether they wait for the Hour to come suddenly; signs have already come, so refusal does not stop arrival.
The source-section root ء ت ي appears in the threat that punishment will surely come suddenly while they are unaware, a specific evil arrival.
The Hour has drawn near (اقْتَرَبَتِ السَّاعَةُ), another direct formulation of the approaching event that opens the image.
When people see a sign they turn away (يُعْرِضُوا); the next ayah identifies this as a refusal of evidence, joining a sign's arrival to turning away.
They deny and follow their desires (كَذَّبُوا وَاتَّبَعُوا أَهْوَاءَهُمْ); this completes 54:2's act of turning away with denial and its eventual settlement.
The source-section root ء ت ي appears in God's command has come (أَتَىٰ أَمْرُ اللَّهِ); people are told not to hasten it, making arrival certain while human timing remains limited.
The source-section root ء ت ي appears as God comes upon the plotters' building from its foundations; this is a distinct punitive arrival.
The source-section root ء ت ي appears in the judgment scene of God coming to people in canopies of cloud with angels; it is a distinct arrival.
The Lord comes with the angels in ranks (وَجَاءَ رَبُّكَ وَالْمَلَكُ صَفًّا صَفًّا), a distinct final-arrival scene beside al-Ghashiya's arrival.
The verse challenges disbelief by reminding people that after life and death they will be returned to God (ثُمَّ إِلَيْهِ تُرْجَعُونَ); disbelief cannot cancel the return.
The question “did you think you would not be returned to Us?” (أَنَّكُمْ إِلَيْنَا لَا تُرْجَعُونَ) directly challenges denial of the destination asserted in 88:25.
Every soul tastes death and then returns to God (ثُمَّ إِلَيْنَا تُرْجَعُونَ); death is a passage to the return, not an escape from it.
God begins creation, repeats it, and people are then returned to Him; the verse connects return to the resurrection that makes judgment possible.
The angel of death takes people, then they are returned to their Lord; this gives the return an explicit passage through death.
At the gathering, each soul faces what it did and is returned to God, its true Master; this makes the return a moment of disclosure.
The source defines awb as returning to one's settled place; “to your Lord that day is the settled destination” (إِلَىٰ رَبِّكَ يَوْمَئِذٍ الْمُسْتَقَرُّ) gives a close semantic parallel.
The deniers call the return “far away” (رَجْعٌ بَعِيدٌ), the explicit contrary claim against the section's certainty that return is to God.
Every soul comes accompanied by a driver and a witness; the arrival is directly staged as a person is brought to account.
The cover is removed from a person's sight (فَكَشَفْنَا عَنكَ غِطَاءَكَ); after the source's covering image, this is the judgment-day unveiling that ends concealment.
The next ayah warns of a near punishment and the day each person will see what their hands sent ahead; it completes 78:39's chosen return with its stakes.
The God-fearing person “comes with a heart turning” (وَجَاءَ بِقَلْبٍ مُّنِيبٍ); arrival and inward voluntary return meet in one phrase.
Whoever wills may take a path to his Lord (اتَّخَذَ إِلَىٰ رَبِّهِ سَبِيلًا); it concretizes choosing a direction of return.
Shuʿayb says “to Him I turn” (وَإِلَيْهِ أُنِيبُ), a personal example of voluntary turning toward God.
When given ease, a person turns away and withdraws to his side, but in hardship despairs; this gives a specific reversal between good arrival and turning away.
After reflecting on the reminder, the opponent turns his back and grows arrogant (ثُمَّ أَدْبَرَ وَاسْتَكْبَرَ); it is a specific refusal-response scene.
The Prophet is told not to let his eyes turn away from those who call on their Lord (وَلَا تَعْدُ عَيْنَاكَ عَنْهُمْ); this is a boundary against abandoning God-oriented companions.
The laid-open record misses nothing, small or great, and the people find their deeds present; this is a specific account-scene parallel to 88:26.
The source-section root ح س ب is used here: Each soul is repaid for what it earned with no injustice, and God is swift in account (سَرِيعُ الْحِسَابِ); it makes the accounting in 88:26 concrete.
Every nation is brought to its record and told it is repaid for what it did; this is a public scene of the reckoning that follows return.
A person has only what he strives for (وَأَن لَّيْسَ لِلْإِنسَانِ إِلَّا مَا سَعَىٰ); the image's satisfied face in 88:9 follows from its effort.
The next ayah says that the effort will be seen, supplying the disclosure before recompense.
The next ayah says the effort will then be fully recompensed, linking 88:9's satisfaction to return and account.
The self-sufficient person transgresses (أَن رَّآهُ اسْتَغْنَىٰ); the next ayah's certain return overturns his imagined independence.
